VERIFICATION OF THE FACTUAL CORE — HOLDS.

1. Quote and numbers are exact and correctly attributed. The source is Lam, Winter, Wei, Xie, Marinov, Bell, "A Large-Scale Longitudinal Study of Flaky Tests," OOPSLA 2020 / Proc. ACM Program. Lang. 4, OOPSLA (DOI 10.1145/3428270) — a top-tier peer-reviewed venue, primary empirical source, from the Illinois MIR group (Marinov) plus Jonathan Bell. I confirmed the "75% of flaky tests (184 out of 245) are flaky when added, indicating substantial potential value for developers to run detectors specifically on newly added tests" sentence against both the authors' PDF (mir.cs.illinois.edu/marinov/publications/LamETAL20LongitudinalFlakyTests.pdf) and the SPLASH/OOPSLA 2020 abstract page. Methodology confirmed: two detectors applied to 55 Java projects, yielding 245 flaky tests that could be compiled and run at the commit where each test was added. Source quality clearly matches claim strength; this is not marketing, not a vendor benchmark, not forum speculation.

2. The prescriptive half of the claim is the authors' OWN stated implication, not an invented extrapolation. "Substantial potential value for developers to run detectors specifically on newly added tests" is verbatim. The claim's hedge — "not only after longitudinal history accumulates" — is also faithful to the paper, which explicitly states that running detectors solely on newly added tests would MISS 25%, rises to 85% when newly-added-or-directly-modified tests are covered, and that the residual 15% become flaky from unrelated changes and are only findable by always running detectors on all tests. The claim does not suppress this; it correctly frames introduction-time detection as additive rather than a replacement.

3. No contradicting source found. I searched for work disputing the "flaky when added" finding and found none. Adjacent work is consistent or complementary, not contradictory (Microsoft's Lam et al. ICSE 2020 lifecycle study; SAP HANA environmental-complexity study; Practical Flaky Test Prediction, arXiv 2302.09330). Industry practice independently corroborates the prescription — Mergify shipped PR-time rerunning of newly added tests, and Atlassian's and Slack's flaky-test tooling posts describe reviewing new tests at merge time.

4. Not outdated in any disqualifying sense. 2020 is six years old, but this remains the canonical citation for flaky-test introduction timing and has not been superseded or retracted; the underlying phenomenon (root-cause distribution of flakiness) is not a fast-moving field.

CAVEATS THAT MUST BE CARRIED — these are why confidence is medium, not high:

A. SEVERE DETECTOR-SCOPE NARROWING. The two detectors are iDFlakies (reruns in randomized test orders → order-dependent, OD) and NonDex (perturbs underdetermined Java-stdlib APIs such as HashMap iteration order → implementation-dependent, ID). I confirmed that NEITHER detects async-wait, concurrency, network, timing, or resource-leak flakiness. Those excluded categories are precisely the dominant real-world causes: Luo et al. (FSE 2014) rank Async Wait and Concurrency above Test Order Dependency, and Microsoft's own lifecycle study of six large proprietary projects names asynchronous calls the LEADING cause. OD and ID flakiness are close to flaky-by-construction — a test that reads HashMap iteration order or depends on residue from another test is that way the instant it is written — so the 75% is measured on the sub-population most biased toward being flaky-at-birth. The unqualified phrase "75% of flaky tests" in the claim is therefore scope-inflated; the defensible statement is "75% of OD/ID flaky tests in Java Maven projects."

B. DENOMINATOR IS A SURVIVORSHIP-FILTERED SUBSET. 245 is not all flaky tests detected; it is those "that can be compiled and run in the code version where each test was added." Flaky tests whose introduction commit would not build were excluded — a second selection effect on top of (A).

C. MECHANISM MISMATCH FOR THE PRODUCT INFERENCE. The claim's parenthetical "(PR/first-run)" is loose. The paper's result comes from purpose-built rerun/perturbation detectors, not from observing a single first execution. A test-intelligence platform that merely watches one first run of a new test detects nothing; realizing this finding requires actually running a detector (N randomized-order reruns, API perturbation, or repeated execution) on new tests at PR time. The roadmap item is therefore "run a detector on newly added tests," not "flag on first run."

D. EXTERNAL-VALIDITY LIMIT RELEVANT TO THIS SPECIFIC PRODUCT. TestLookup ingests Cypress, Playwright, Robot, and Cucumber — UI/E2E suites where async-wait dominates (cf. the ICSE 2021 UI-based flaky test study). The 55-project Java/Maven sample supports the shift-left principle but does NOT license the 75% number as a forecast of what an introduction-time detector would catch in those suites.

NET: the claim is well-sourced, accurately quoted, numerically correct, and its recommendation is the authors' own — so it is not refuted. It should be restated with the OD/ID + Java scoping and the "run a detector, not just watch one run" mechanism made explicit before it drives a roadmap decision.

Sources: https://mir.cs.illinois.edu/marinov/publications/LamETAL20LongitudinalFlakyTests.pdf ; https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3428270 ; https://2020.splashcon.org/details/splash-2020-oopsla/78/A-Large-Scale-Longitudinal-Study-of-Flaky-Tests ; https://mir.cs.illinois.edu/lamyaa/publications/fse14.pdf ; https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/a-study-on-the-lifecycle-of-flaky-tests/ ; https://taoxie.cs.illinois.edu/publications/icst19-idflakies.pdf ; https://weihang-wang.github.io/papers/UIFlaky-icse21.pdf
verdicts.counterSource: No source contradicts the finding. The strongest qualifying evidence is detector-coverage scope: iDFlakies detects only order-dependent flakiness and NonDex only implementation-dependent flakiness from underdetermined Java-stdlib APIs (https://taoxie.cs.illinois.edu/publications/icst19-idflakies.pdf), so the 245-test sample excludes async-wait/concurrency/network/timing flakiness — the categories ranked most common by Luo et al. FSE 2014 (https://mir.cs.illinois.edu/lamyaa/publications/fse14.pdf) and named the leading cause in Microsoft's six-project lifecycle study (https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/a-study-on-the-lifecycle-of-flaky-tests/). The paper's own counterweight: detectors run solely on newly added tests miss 25%; 85% with directly-modified tests included; the residual 15% require always-on detection across all tests.

verdicts.claim: Extending detection to directly modified tests raises coverage to 85%, but the remaining 15% of flaky tests become flaky due to changes made elsewhere (code under test, other tests, dependencies) and can only be caught by continuously applying detection to all tests — meaning new/modified-test-only strategies (as used at Mozilla and Netflix) have a measurable, quantified blind spot.
verdicts.evidence:
VERIFICATION ATTEMPTS (adversarial):

1. Quote fidelity — CONFIRMED, not an overreach. Direct PDF fetch failed (compressed content streams), but two independent retrievals of the paper's content reproduced the finding verbatim: "The percentage of flaky tests that can be detected does increase to 85% when detectors are run on newly added or directly modified tests. The remaining 15% of flaky tests become flaky due to other changes and can be detected only when detectors are always applied to all tests." The baseline the 85% extends is also confirmed: 184/245 (75%) of flaky tests were already flaky when added. The claim's paraphrase ("raises coverage to 85%") matches; "can only be caught by continuously applying detection to all tests" is near-verbatim.

2. The Mozilla/Netflix attribution — CONFIRMED as the PAPER'S OWN framing, not an inference bolted on by the claim: "Some software organizations, e.g., Mozilla and Netflix, run some tools—detectors—to detect flaky tests as soon as possible. However, these organizations typically run a detector solely on newly added or directly modified tests, i.e., not on unmodified tests or when other changes occur (including changes to the test suite, the code under test, and library dependencies)." So the "blind spot" conclusion is the paper's stated motivation, not the claim's editorializing.

3. Source strength — MATCHES claim strength. Lam, Winter, Wei, Xie, Marinov, Bell; Proc. ACM Program. Lang. Vol 4, OOPSLA, Nov 2020 (DOI 10.1145/3428270); peer-reviewed top-tier venue, vendor-neutral academic, not a press release or benchmark.

4. Contradicting evidence — NONE FOUND. Searches for studies disputing the 85/15 split returned only work that reinforces it (environmental-flakiness studies, SAP HANA 2024, JS environmental-flakiness evaluation): tests demonstrably become flaky from dependency updates, OS/hardware/browser/resource variation with zero test-code change. That error direction makes the 15% blind spot LARGER, not smaller — it cannot refute a claim that a blind spot exists.

5. Outdated? 2020, six years old, but this is a historical empirical measurement of open-source commit histories, not a fast-decaying technology claim; it remains the canonical citation. The only genuinely stale element is the present-tense characterization of Mozilla's/Netflix's 2026 practice — the paper describes 2020 practice secondhand — but the quantified finding does not depend on it.

MATERIAL SCOPE CAVEAT (report the figures with scope, not as universal constants): the numbers derive from 245 flaky tests across 55 Java/Maven projects, detected by iDFlakies (order-dependent) plus NonDex (implementation-dependent) — a detector set biased toward OD/ID flakiness (iDFlakies datasets run ~50% order-dependent) and largely blind to async-wait/concurrency/UI flakiness that dominates other taxonomies. So "85%" is not a language- or domain-general constant; for JS/Python/UI/e2e suites the new-and-modified-only strategy plausibly covers far less. The claim's directional conclusion survives; only the precision of "85%/15%" outside Java/Maven should be hedged.
verdicts.counterSource: No refuting source found. Nearest qualifiers (which amplify rather than contradict the blind spot): "Do Test and Environmental Complexity Increase Flakiness? An Empirical Study of SAP HANA" (arXiv 2409.10062) and "A Systematic Evaluation of Environmental Flakiness in JavaScript Tests" (arXiv 2602.19098), both documenting flakiness arising with no test-code change. The only real weakness is scope: iDFlakies (ICST'19) datasets are ~50% order-dependent, so the detector pair used biases the population toward OD/ID flakiness.

verdicts.claim: Extending detection to directly modified tests raises coverage to 85%, but the remaining 15% of flaky tests become flaky due to changes made elsewhere (code under test, other tests, dependencies) and can only be caught by continuously applying detection to all tests — meaning new/modified-test-only strategies (as used at Mozilla and Netflix) have a measurable, quantified blind spot.
verdicts.evidence:
VERIFIED AGAINST PRIMARY SOURCE. I downloaded the PDF (Lam, Winter, Wei, Xie, Marinov, Bell — "A Large-Scale Longitudinal Study of Flaky Tests," Proc. ACM Program. Lang. Vol 4, OOPSLA, Article 202, Nov 2020) and extracted its text rather than relying on search summaries.

1. QUOTE IS VERBATIM AND CORRECTLY READ. Abstract, lines 25-28 of extracted text: "running detectors solely on newly added tests would still miss detecting 25% of flaky tests. The percentage of flaky tests that can be detected does increase to 85% when detectors are run on newly added or directly modified tests. The remaining 15% of flaky tests become flaky due to other changes and can be detected only when detectors are always applied to all tests." No paraphrase drift.

2. THE UNDERLYING ARITHMETIC CHECKS OUT IN THE BODY (Section 6, lines 972-979): "we find that 75% of flaky tests in our study are detected as flaky on their TIC [test introduction commit]... we further find that 24 of 61 (39%) tests not flaky on their TIC become flaky in a commit that changes the code of the class containing the flaky test. Combining these 24 tests and the 184 tests that are flaky when they are added, we find that 208 of 245 (85%) tests can be detected by running flaky-test detectors on newly added or existing, but directly modified tests. However, it still leaves 15% of flaky tests that become flaky due to changes not being directly in the test class itself but rather elsewhere in the test suite, code under test, or library dependencies." 184+24=208; 208/245=84.9%. The claim's characterization of the 15% blind spot ("code under test, other tests, dependencies") is a near-verbatim restatement of the paper's own enumeration, not an inference.

3. THE MOZILLA/NETFLIX ATTRIBUTION IS THE PAPER'S OWN, NOT THE CLAIMANT'S EMBELLISHMENT. Abstract: "Some software organizations, e.g., Mozilla and Netflix, run some tools—detectors—to detect flaky tests as soon as possible... these organizations typically run a detector solely on newly added or directly modified tests, i.e., not on unmodified tests or when other changes occur (including changes to the test suite, the code under test, and library dependencies)." Section 6 (line 970) adds the concrete instance: "Mozilla runs its 'test verification' [MozillaChaosMode 2019] only on tests newly added or modified in a commit." This was the most likely overreach vector and it survives.

4. SOURCE QUALITY MATCHES CLAIM STRENGTH. Peer-reviewed OOPSLA/PACMPL paper, not a vendor blog, press release, or forum post. Authors are the core academic flaky-test group (Marinov/Bell/Lam — also authors of iDFlakies and RootFinder). Claim is a modest, quantified empirical finding, not extraordinary.

5. NO CONTRADICTING EVIDENCE FOUND. Searched for replications, disputes, and later work challenging the 85/15 split; found none. Subsequent literature (FlakeFlagger, Flakify, Parry et al. "Systemic Flakiness" 2025, SAP HANA studies) builds on rather than disputes it. The nearest adjacent challenge, Haben et al. ASE 2024 ("The Importance of Accounting for Execution Failures when Predicting Test Flakiness"), disputes flaky-vs-fault-revealing classification — an orthogonal question, not the introduction-timing split.

6. NOT OUTDATED IN A DISQUALIFYING WAY. 2020 paper, but the claim concerns the causal structure of when flakiness is introduced (test-local vs. environmental/dependency change), which is not a fast-moving-field claim in the sense that LLM tooling benchmarks are. Mozilla's test-verification policy and the detector-cost economics that motivate new/modified-only strategies still hold.

CAVEATS THAT QUALIFY BUT DO NOT REFUTE — the roadmap should carry these: (a) Population is 245 flaky tests across 55 Java/Maven open-source projects, found by only two detectors (iDFlakies + NonDex, operationalized as Isolation, One-By-One, and NonDex). The paper concedes in §8.1.2: "the flaky tests that we study come from only two detectors... these detectors do not guarantee the detection of every flaky test." (b) That detector set skews the sample toward order-dependent and implementation-dependent flakiness — of 432 categorized tests, 155 OD-victim, 23 OD-brittle, 190 implementation-dependent, but only 64 non-deterministic. Async-wait/concurrency/network flakiness, which dominates practitioner reports, is under-sampled, so 85/15 should NOT be generalized to "all flaky tests in any stack." (c) §8.1.3 explicitly states "The results from our study may not generalize to a larger population of projects, flaky tests, or flaky-test detectors." (d) The claim drops the paper's own scoping phrase "of the flaky tests that we study." (e) The paper separately notes a latency cost the claim omits: detecting via test-class modification arrives a median 61 commits / 22 days after the test's introduction commit. Recommend the finding be cited as "85%/15% among order- and implementation-dependent flaky tests in 55 Java OSS projects (Lam et al., OOPSLA 2020)" rather than as a universal constant.
verdicts.counterSource: No contradicting source found. Nearest adjacent challenge: Haben et al., "The Importance of Accounting for Execution Failures when Predicting Test Flakiness," ASE 2024 (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3691620.3695261) — disputes flaky-vs-fault-revealing failure classification, not the introduction-timing split; does not contradict this claim. Parry et al., "Systemic Flakiness," EASE 2025 (https://arxiv.org/html/2504.16777) argues per-test cause categorization may report a skewed cause distribution, which mildly qualifies the sample composition but not the 85/15 timing result.

verdicts.claim: 75% of flaky tests (184 of 245 studied) are already flaky at the commit that introduces the test, so running flaky-test detectors on newly added tests catches the large majority of flakiness at the moment it is cheapest to fix — a test-intelligence platform should therefore flag flakiness at test-introduction time (PR/first-run), not only after longitudinal history accumulates.
verdicts.evidence:
The NUMBER is real; the ACTIONABLE CONCLUSION is refuted. I extracted the primary PDF (29pp, Lam/Winter/Wei/Xie/Marinov/Bell, OOPSLA 2020, PACMPL 4:202) and confirmed the quote verbatim at line 742: "Of the 245 flaky tests, 184 tests (75%) are detected as flaky tests on their TIC." So clause 1 is accurate. Four independent grounds refute the inference drawn from it:

(1) DENOMINATOR: the paper detected 684 potentially flaky tests, confirmed 432, and could only compile/run 245 at the test-introducing commit — "we are able to run only 245 of the total 432 (684-252) confirmed flaky tests on their TIC." So 184/684 = 27% of all detected flaky tests, not "the large majority of flakiness." The 252 excluded UD tests are explicitly those whose flakiness "was not possible to ever reproduce ... outside of the full test suite" — i.e. precisely the environment-sensitive kind that dominates real CI. That is survivorship bias toward reproducible-in-isolation tests.

(2) CATEGORY BIAS DRIVES THE 75%: of 432 categorized tests, 190 ID + 155 OD-Vic + 23 OD-Brit = 85%, while non-deterministic (ND) is only 64 (15%). The paper's own causal explanation (line 874): "OD Brits, NDs, and IDs, which are all tests that, when each is run by itself, can result in a flaky-test failure, do have a high likelihood to be detected in their TICs." The high rate is an artifact of a population dominated by intrinsic, self-contained, deterministically-reproducible flakiness (e.g. HashSet iteration order). Luo et al. FSE 2014 found real-world flakiness is 45% async-wait and 20% concurrency — categories structurally absent here, and the paper warns of ND results: "no robust detectors for ND tests exist, so this result may not generalize."

(3) "PR/FIRST-RUN" MISREPRESENTS THE METHOD: detection at TIC required iDFlakies permuting the entire suite, One-By-One (running the test after every other test), NonDex API randomization, and in confirmation cases 500 runs ("confirming with 500 runs"). Mozilla's cited practice is "10 isolated runs and 5 other additional isolated runs, each in a new execution environment." None of this is observable from a first run; a platform that ingests JUnit/pytest XML passively cannot implement this finding at all without an active rerun/shuffle harness.

(4) THE PAPER ITSELF CONTRADICTS THE FRAMING, AND SO DOES INDUSTRY: line 850 — "running the detector only on the TIC may provide a false sense of safety." Abstract: 15% "can be detected only when detectors are always applied to all tests." The claim's "not only after longitudinal history accumulates" inverts this. Industrially, Li Haoyi (built Databricks' CI flaky metric, Dropbox Changes CI) reports the opposite: "the majority of flaky tests we detected were existing tests that were stable for days/weeks/months before turning flaky," and "To block code changes that cause either new and old tests from becoming flaky, we would need to run every single test about 300 times on each pull request...This is prohibitively slow and expensive," concluding "it is very hard to block flaky tests 'up front.'"

Also: "cheapest to fix" is asserted, never measured — the paper measures detection cost/timing, not remediation cost. And scope is 55 Maven/Java OSS projects on a 2019 snapshot; TestLookup ingests Cypress/Playwright/Robot/pytest, ecosystems where async-timing flakiness dominates and this distribution does not hold.
verdicts.counterSource: https://mill-build.org/blog/4-flaky-tests.html (Li Haoyi, Databricks/Dropbox CI); Luo et al. FSE 2014 https://mir.cs.illinois.edu/lamyaa/publications/fse14.pdf; plus the primary paper's own Section 5 / RQ2 text

verdicts.claim: Flaky-test prevalence at scale is high enough to be a first-class product problem: Google reported roughly 16% of its tests were flaky (with about 1 in 7 tests written by engineers occasionally failing), and GitHub reported in 2020 that about 9% of commits (one in eleven) had at least one red build caused by a flaky test — so a test-intelligence platform must treat flakiness as a routine, high-volume signal-quality issue, not an edge case.
verdicts.evidence:
Both numbers trace to verifiable PRIMARY sources, not just the arXiv survey (2212.00908), which is a peer-reviewed multivocal review (published in Information & Software Technology / ScienceDirect) merely relaying them.

(1) GOOGLE — verified verbatim at testing.googleblog.com "Flaky Tests at Google and How We Mitigate Them" (John Micco, May 27, 2016), fetched via the googblogs mirror: "Almost 16% of our tests have some level of flakiness associated with them!" and "it means that more than 1 in 7 of the tests written by our world-class engineers occasionally fail in a way not caused by changes". Same post: "about 1.5% of all test runs reporting a 'flaky' result" and "about 84% of the transitions we observe from pass to fail involve a flaky test". The survey's paraphrase is faithful (if anything Google said "more than 1 in 7").

(2) GITHUB — verified verbatim at github.blog/2020-12-16-reducing-flaky-builds-by-18x (Dec 16, 2020): "Earlier this year in our monolith, 1 in 11 commits had at least one red build caused by a flaky test, or about 9 percent of commits." Exactly as claimed, correctly dated.

Adversarial checks that did NOT refute it: I searched for contradicting/qualifying sources and found no credible source disputing either figure. Independent corroboration of the "routine, not edge case" conclusion exists (Google 2017 "Where do our flaky tests come from?"; the Chromium CI study arXiv 2302.10594; ~13% of GitHub-project build failures attributed to flaky tests).

Three QUALIFICATIONS the roadmap should carry, none of which falsify the claim:
(a) SEMANTICS — 16% is a cumulative "has ever shown some flakiness" inventory measure, not a concurrent state. Google's own concurrent figures are ~1.5% of test *runs* and ~62k of 4.2M tests (~1.5%) flaky in a given week. "16% of its tests were flaky" reads as instantaneous and overstates the steady-state rate ~10x.
(b) CHERRY-PICK RISK — GitHub's 9% is the *before* number in a post about an 18x reduction; six weeks after shipping flaky-test management it fell to "less than half a percent, or 1 in 200 commits." Quoting only 9% implies the problem is inevitable when GitHub's own data says dedicated tooling collapses it (which actually supports building the product, but the "after" number must be cited alongside).
(c) GENERALIZABILITY — these are hyperscale monorepo numbers. Academic open-source studies (e.g. the PyPI study over 22,352 projects, arXiv 2101.09077) find far lower per-test flakiness (~0.5–1%), so "high prevalence" is scale-dependent and may not hold for the small self-hosted teams TestLookup targets.
(d) AGE — 2016 and 2020 data cited in 2026; no refreshed Google figure exists, though flakiness prevalence is not a fast-moving quantity and later work (2023–2026) continues to find it a dominant share of CI failures.
verdicts.counterSource: https://github.blog/2020-12-16-reducing-flaky-builds-by-18x/ (same post reports the 9% dropped to <0.5% / 1-in-200 after mitigation — partial counter to the "routine, inevitable" framing); https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.09077 (open-source flaky rates ~0.5–1%, far below 16%, limiting generalization beyond hyperscale monorepos)

verdicts.claim: The dominant cost of flakiness is erosion of trust in the test signal itself — practitioners report that once confidence is lost, the test suite loses its value entirely, which is why a reporting tool's core job is preserving signal trustworthiness (clearly separating flaky from real failures) rather than just displaying results.
verdicts.evidence:
REFUTED on three independent grounds: source misattribution, contradiction by the cited paper itself, and contradiction by primary empirical work.

1) SOURCE MISATTRIBUTION — the "primary source" is a secondary citation of a vendor blog. arXiv 2212.00908 is Rasheed, Tahir, Dietrich, Hashemi & Zhang, "Test Flakiness' Causes, Detection, Impact and Responses: A Multivocal Review" (Dec 2022, JSS 2023) — a literature review over 651 articles (560 academic + 91 grey-literature posts). Fetching the HTML (ar5iv) confirms the supporting quote sits in Section 4.5.2, the GREY-LITERATURE impact analysis, attributed to Spotify Engineering (Table 9, ref [1]) — i.e. the 2019 Spotify blog post "Test Flakiness – Methods for identifying and dealing with flaky tests." Web search independently confirms the exact wording originates from that Spotify post. So the claim is built on one engineering-blog rhetorical assertion, quoted verbatim inside a review, not on primary empirical measurement. Calling it "primary" is false, and "practitioners report" (plural, survey-like) misrepresents a single blog author's opinion.

2) THE CITED PAPER ITSELF DOES NOT SUPPORT "DOMINANT." The review does NOT rank trust erosion as the dominant cost. It organizes impacts into six unranked categories (academic: product quality 10, testing techniques 14, debugging/maintenance 6; grey: product/codebase 5, developers 6, delivery 8), with productivity loss, time waste and deployment slowdown cited alongside lost trust. Direct answer from the paper's impact section: it "does not claim trust erosion is the dominant cost… presents trust/confidence issues as one among many."

3) CONTRADICTED BY THE STRONGEST PRIMARY EVIDENCE. Habchi et al., "A Qualitative Study on the Sources, Impacts, and Mitigation Strategies of Flaky Tests" (arXiv 2112.04919, ICST 2022, 14 practitioner interviews) finds the opposite ranking: "Wasting developer time is perceived as the most severe consequence of test flakiness" (participant: "in a CI today with 400 deliveries per day, disruptions waste so much time"). Trust erosion appears as a real but secondary/downstream effect. A claim asserting a DOMINANT cost is refuted when the actual interview study ranks a different cost first.

4) "LOSES ITS VALUE ENTIRELY" IS HYPERBOLE CONTRADICTED BY PRACTICE. Google reports ~1.5% of test runs flaky affecting ~16% of tests, and 84% of pass→fail transitions involve a flaky test — yet Google's suite demonstrably still delivers value via reruns, quarantine and flakiness scoring. If "no better position than zero tests" were literally true, every large CI system operating at nonzero flake rates would be worthless, which is false. The quote is rhetorical framing, not a measured finding.

5) THE PRODUCT INFERENCE IS UNSUPPORTED BY THE QUOTE. The clause "which is why a reporting tool's core job is preserving signal trustworthiness… rather than just displaying results" is a normative roadmap conclusion nowhere present in the quote or the paper; the quote says nothing about reporting tools. Note the surviving directionally-true kernel worth keeping (with correct sourcing): trust erosion is a REAL and well-documented impact — Habchi's broken-window finding (developers become lenient, "get away with it"), and Microsoft's finding that developers who hit flaky tests are less likely to investigate subsequent failures. But that supports "trust erosion is one significant cost, and flaky/real separation is a valuable feature," NOT "dominant cost" + "value entirely" + "core job."
verdicts.counterSource: Habchi et al., "A Qualitative Study on the Sources, Impacts, and Mitigation Strategies of Flaky Tests," ICST 2022 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.04919) — ranks wasted developer time, not trust loss, as the most severe consequence; plus the cited review's own Section 4.5.2 / Tables 8-9 (https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2212.00908), which attributes the quote to the Spotify Engineering blog (https://engineering.atspotify.com/2019/11/test-flakiness-methods-for-identifying-and-dealing-with-flaky-tests) and presents trust as one unranked impact among many.

verdicts.claim: The dominant cost of flakiness is erosion of trust in the test signal itself — practitioners report that once confidence is lost, the test suite loses its value entirely, which is why a reporting tool's core job is preserving signal trustworthiness (clearly separating flaky from real failures) rather than just displaying results.
verdicts.evidence:
REFUTED on four independent grounds.

1) SOURCE MISATTRIBUTION — the cited "primary" source is not primary. arXiv 2212.00908 (Rasheed, Tahir, Dietrich, Hashemi, Zhang, "Test Flakiness' Causes, Detection, Impact and Responses: A Multivocal Review", Dec 2022) is a literature review, not an empirical study. The supporting quote appears in §4.5.2 as a verbatim block quotation attributed to **Spotify Engineering** and catalogued in the paper's **grey-literature** table (Table 9), i.e. a company engineering blog post ("Test Flakiness — Methods for identifying and dealing with flaky tests", Spotify Labs, Nov 2019). The review reports it as one voice among many documented impacts and supplies **no frequency counts**; it never endorses confidence loss as the dominant cost. Presenting a 2019 vendor blog aphorism as an arXiv primary finding is exactly the source-strength mismatch the checklist targets.

2) "DOMINANT COST" CONTRADICTED BY THE PRACTITIONER DATA. Habchi et al., "A Qualitative Study on the Sources, Impacts, and Mitigation Strategies of Flaky Tests" (arXiv 2112.04919): impact ranking across practitioners is (1) wasted developer time 10/14 = 71%, (2) CI disruption 7/14 = 50%, (3) affects testing practices 6/14 = 43%, (4) undermines system reliability/distrust 5/14 = 36%, (5) disguises bugs 2/14 = 14%. Trust erosion ranks BELOW time/CI cost. Gruber & Fraser, "A Survey on How Test Flakiness Affects Developers…" (arXiv 2203.00483, n=335 professionals) independently reproduces this: highest-rated consequence is "wasting developer time" (mean 2.44/4), ahead of rerunning-without-analysis (2.08), PR-merge friction (2.08) and wasted compute (1.91). Two independent studies rank time/throughput cost above trust. Trust erosion is real but is NOT "the dominant cost."

3) "THE SUITE LOSES ITS VALUE ENTIRELY" IS FALSIFIED, NOT MERELY UNPROVEN. Gruber & Fraser find trust loss is **asymmetric**: developers lose confidence in test *failures* significantly more than in test *passes* (p<0.001), and they keep using the suites — "developers mostly fall back to rerunning and rewriting test cases," i.e. persistent engagement, not abandonment. Google operates at ~1.5% per-run flake rate with ~16% of tests exhibiting some flakiness and the suite remains foundational to its engineering; Google's own testing-blog data reports the opposite of worthlessness — suites in the 0.1–1% flake band showed *lower* bug discovery, with crashes/unexpected exits higher on higher-flake tests, implying flaky tests are partly signal. "No better position than a team that has zero tests" is blog rhetoric contradicted by the behavioural and outcome evidence.

4) THE PRESCRIPTIVE CLAUSE IS AN UNSOURCED NON SEQUITUR. Neither the multivocal review nor the Spotify post says anything about what a reporting tool's "core job" is. "…which is why a reporting tool's core job is preserving signal trustworthiness rather than just displaying results" is the analyst's product inference smuggled in under a citation that does not support it.

WHAT SURVIVES (weaker, still usable): flakiness measurably erodes trust in failing results specifically, and distrusted failures let real bugs through (Habchi 5/14; Microsoft/Lam et al. find developers who hit flaky tests are less likely to investigate subsequent failures). A defensible restatement: "Flakiness imposes its largest measured cost in wasted developer time and CI disruption, and a secondary but compounding cost in asymmetric distrust of failing results — so separating flaky from real failures is one high-value job for a reporting tool." The claim as written (dominant cost, total loss of value, therefore core job) is overreach.

verdicts.claim: Unmanaged flakiness compounds into organizational failure: the review cites organizations that reached 50%+ flaky tests, at which point developers stopped writing tests and stopped looking at results — evidence that flaky-test management (detection + quarantine lifecycle + burn-down) is a productivity feature, not a nice-to-have.
verdicts.evidence: MISATTRIBUTED VENDOR MARKETING, NOT A PRIMARY FINDING. (1) Provenance: arXiv 2212.00908 (Rasheed, Tahir, Dietrich, Hashemi, Zhang, "Test Flakiness' Causes, Detection, Impact and Responses: A Multivocal Review", Dec 2022) is a literature review of 651 articles (560 academic + 91 GREY literature). The ar5iv full text confirms the quote appears there ONLY as a quoted grey-literature datapoint, attributed in its Table 9 grey-lit set to a Datadog product manager — i.e. the review reports the statement, it does not measure or validate it. Labelling arXiv 2212.00908 as the "primary" source for this claim is a provenance error. (2) The real origin is a product-marketing blog: "We Have A Flaky Test Problem" by Bryan Lee, Product Manager at Undefined Labs (maker of Scope, later acquired by Datadog), published 9 Dec 2019 on Medium/dev.to. It closes with the CTA "Your journey to better engineering through better testing starts with Scope" — i.e. a vendor selling flaky-test tooling asserting that flaky-test tooling is essential. Fails checklist item 5. (3) Anecdotal with zero method: "We've talked to some organizations" — no N, no sampling, no definition of "50%+ flaky tests in their codebase" (50% of tests? of runs? of failures?), no measurement of the alleged behavioral outcome. Fails checklist item 3: an extraordinary "half the suite is flaky, developers abandoned testing" claim is carried by a second-hand sales anecdote. (4) Magnitude contradicted by measured industrial data: Google reports ~1.5% of test EXECUTIONS flaky (16% of tests show some flakiness over their lifetime, per the Google Testing Blog / "Advances in Continuous Integration Testing @Google"); Microsoft's large-scale studies (Lam et al., RootFinder) put flaky behavior at ~4.6% of tests with ~27% of builds affected. A 50%+ flaky codebase is an order of magnitude beyond anything measured in published industrial studies — an unverified outlier, not a representative organizational trajectory. (5) The causal endpoint is unevidenced: peer-reviewed qualitative work (Eck et al. 2019 "Understanding Flaky Tests: The Developer's Perspective", arXiv 1907.01466; Habchi et al. arXiv 2112.04919) documents loss of trust, reruns, deprioritization and ignoring of flaky tests — not organizations where "developers stopped writing tests." The specific "organizational failure" outcome rests solely on the vendor anecdote. (6) Overreach beyond the quote: the quote says nothing about "compounding," and nothing about the prescribed remedy (detection + quarantine lifecycle + burn-down); that remedy framing is added by the claim, matching the product being built rather than the cited evidence. NOTE FOR THE ROADMAP: the directional thesis that flakiness erodes trust in CI signal and costs QA productivity IS defensible — but it must be sourced to Google/Microsoft measured data and the peer-reviewed qualitative studies above, not to a 2019 Scope/Datadog sales anecdote presented as an arXiv primary finding. Use as written and the roadmap cites a competitor's marketing copy as research.

verdicts.evidence: MISLABELED SOURCE + MARKETING ORIGIN. (1) The quote IS in arXiv 2212.00908 (Rasheed/Tahir/Dietrich, "Test Flakiness' Causes, Detection, Impact and Responses: A Multivocal Review", JSS 206:111837, 2023) — I extracted the PDF text and confirmed it verbatim. But the paper does NOT assert it; it quotes it as grey literature: "...as this is the case with some organisations: 'We've talked to some organizations that reached 50%+ flaky tests...' (Product Manager at Datadog, [G3])". [G3] is a grey-lit entry. The claim labels arXiv 2212.00908 "(primary)" — it is not primary for this fact; it is a secondary report of a vendor blog. Multivocal reviews include grey literature by design WITHOUT validating its empirical basis. (2) The actual origin is "We Have A Flaky Test Problem" by Bryan Lee of Undefined Labs (dev.to/kickingthetv/we-have-a-flaky-test-problem-11ol, 9 Dec 2019; also on Medium/@scopedev). Undefined Labs sold CI test observability and was acquired by Datadog — the speaker's company sells the flaky-test-management product the claim concludes is essential. I fetched the post: it cites specific Google research for other stats (84% of test transitions from flaky tests, 16% of tests have some flakiness) but supplies ZERO data, no named organizations, and no definition of how "50%+ flaky" was measured for this anecdote. Textbook self-serving vendor anecdote. (3) The 50%+ figure is an unreplicated extreme outlier vs. every published measurement: Google ~16% of tests exhibit some flakiness (~1.5% flaky), Microsoft ~26% of pass/fail transitions, and empirical studies (FlakeFlagger, JS flakiness studies) report single-digit percentages. Nothing in the peer-reviewed literature corroborates a 50%+ flaky codebase. (4) Age: the underlying anecdote is Dec 2019, ~7 years old, predating the current flaky-management tooling generation. (5) The overreach: the claim promotes hearsay-of-hearsay ("we've talked to some organizations") into a causal organizational-failure narrative and then calls it "evidence" for a product requirement. NOTE FOR THE ROADMAP: the CONCLUSION (flaky management is a productivity feature, not nice-to-have) is independently well-supported — Parry et al. survey (arXiv 2203.00483), Eck et al. 2019 developer perceptions, GitLab's public flaky-test handbook, Google/Microsoft trust-erosion data — so cite THOSE. This specific claim-plus-citation should be dropped or rewritten as an illustrative vendor anecdote, never as primary evidence.

verdicts.claim: Flaky-test prevalence at scale is high enough to be a first-class product problem: Google reported roughly 16% of its tests were flaky (with about 1 in 7 tests written by engineers occasionally failing), and GitHub reported in 2020 that about 9% of commits (one in eleven) had at least one red build caused by a flaky test — so a test-intelligence platform must treat flakiness as a routine, high-volume signal-quality issue, not an edge case.
verdicts.evidence:
The two numbers exist verbatim, but the claim's construction of them is materially misleading on three counts, two of which are self-contradicted by the claim's own cited primary sources.

1) THE GITHUB HALF IS A PRE-FIX BASELINE THAT THE SAME ARTICLE REPORTS WAS ELIMINATED. I fetched the cited source (https://github.blog/2020-12-16-reducing-flaky-builds-by-18x/). It says "1 in 11 commits had at least one red build caused by a flaky test, or about 9 percent of commits" — but that is explicitly the BEFORE state ("earlier in 2020"), and the same post continues: "the percentage of commits with flaky builds dropped to less than half a percent, or 1 in 200 commits" about six weeks after they shipped their flaky-test management system, calling it "an 18x improvement and the lowest rate of flaky builds since we began tracking flaky tests in 2016." The article's conclusion is that 9% was fixable down to 0.5%; the claim cites the 9% as if it characterized GitHub's steady state. The title of the source is literally "Reducing flaky builds by 18x."

2) THE "16%" AND "1 IN 7" ARE THE SAME NUMBER RESTATED, NOT TWO DATA POINTS, AND ARE 10-YEAR-OLD GREY LITERATURE. Traced to the actual primary source (John Micco, Google Testing Blog, MAY 2016): "Almost 16% of our tests have some level of flakiness associated with them!" and, in the very next sentence, "it means that more than 1 in 7 of the tests written by our world-class engineers occasionally fail." 1/7 = 14.3% — it is the same measurement paraphrased, so the claim's "16% ... with about 1 in 7 ..." presents no independent corroboration. It is also a 2016 blog post (no methodology, no dataset, single monorepo), not a primary research artifact, and the claim's cited source (arXiv 2212.00908) is itself a secondary multivocal literature review (Rasheed, Tahir, Dietrich, Hashemi, Zhang — JSS, 2022) that merely reprints the blog figure. The claim is 2016+2020 data used to assert the 2026 state of the world.

3) THE 16% IS CONTRADICTED AS A GENERAL PREVALENCE RATE BY PEER-REVIEWED LARGE-SCALE MEASUREMENT. Gruber et al., "An Empirical Study of Flaky Tests in Python" (ICST 2021, arXiv 2101.09077): 22,352 PyPI projects, 876,186 test cases, 7,571 flaky tests = 0.86% of tests flaky, and only 4.5% of projects contained ANY flaky test — roughly 19x below the headline figure, and it directly undercuts "routine, high-volume" as a description of typical (non-hyperscaler) codebases.

4) THE SAME GOOGLE POST CARRIES THE OPERATIONALLY RELEVANT NUMBER, WHICH IS AN ORDER OF MAGNITUDE SMALLER: "Across our entire corpus of tests, we see a continual rate of about 1.5% of all test runs reporting a 'flaky' result." 16% is "any flakiness ever observed over a long window," not per-run incidence; the claim's paraphrase "16% of its tests were flaky" silently drops Google's "some level of flakiness associated with them" hedge.

WHAT SURVIVES: the directional thesis is defensible, but on different evidence than cited — specifically Google's "About 84% of the transitions we observe from pass to fail involve a flaky test" (same 2016 post), which is a signal-quality argument rather than a prevalence argument. The claim as written should not be used: the GitHub 9% must either be dropped or stated with its 0.5% post-fix outcome, the 16%/1-in-7 pair must be collapsed into one 2016 Google-specific data point with its "some level of flakiness" qualifier, and any general-prevalence framing must be reconciled with the 0.86% peer-reviewed figure.

Also noted: 2025-26 searches for current prevalence returned almost exclusively vendor SEO content (TestDino, Bug0, Functionize, AccelQ, Keploy, scrolltest), i.e. no credible refreshed primary measurement was found to rescue the claim's currency.

verdicts.claim: Unmanaged flakiness compounds into organizational failure: the review cites organizations that reached 50%+ flaky tests, at which point developers stopped writing tests and stopped looking at results — evidence that flaky-test management (detection + quarantine lifecycle + burn-down) is a productivity feature, not a nice-to-have.
verdicts.evidence:
CITATION LAUNDERING — the quote is not a finding of the arXiv review. Verified via ar5iv (https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2212.00908): the sentence appears in Rasheed et al., "Test Flakiness' Causes, Detection, Impact and Responses: A Multivocal Review," Section 4.5.2 "Impact noted in grey literature" (Table 9, ref [3]) — a section whose explicit purpose is to CATALOGUE practitioner claims separately from academic evidence, not to endorse them. The claim says "the review cites organizations that reached 50%+ flaky tests"; the review cites a blog post that claims to have talked to unnamed organizations. That is a second-hand, unverified anecdote re-presented as an academic citation.

THE UNDERLYING SOURCE IS VENDOR MARKETING. Verified via https://dev.to/kickingthetv/we-have-a-flaky-test-problem-11ol (Dec 2019, mirrored at medium.com/scopedev): author is Bryan Lee, Product Manager at Undefined Labs, and the post is a product ad for Scope — it closes with "Scope gives engineering teams production-level visibility" and the CTA "Your journey to better engineering through better testing starts with Scope." Undefined Labs was acquired by Datadog (Scope became Datadog Test Optimization) — i.e. the source is one of the exact competitor vendors named in the research brief, selling the precise remedy ("flaky-test management ... detection + quarantine lifecycle") that the claim concludes is essential. Self-serving marketing anecdote in support of buying/building the thing the author sells.

NO DATA BEHIND THE 50% FIGURE. The post gives no named organization, no count of organizations ("some organizations"), no sample, no methodology, and no operational definition of "flaky test." Nothing is measurable or falsifiable.

CONTRADICTED BY EVERY MEASURED DISTRIBUTION. 50%+ of a codebase being flaky is a wild outlier vs. instrumented data: Google — ~16% of 4.2M tests showed SOME flakiness, with weekly rates of 0.5% (small), 1.6% (medium), 14% (large); Meta — ~10% for E2E, well below 1% for unit. The frequently-cited Microsoft "14%–52%" range is the percentage of BUILDS in which a flaky test was observed, not the percentage of tests that are flaky — a different denominator that is often misread to make figures like 50% sound normal. No dataset supports a 50%-of-tests regime, so the anecdote cannot function as a threshold or tipping point.

BEHAVIORAL CONSEQUENCE ASSERTED, NOT OBSERVED. "Developers stopped writing tests and stopped looking at results" is the blogger's characterization, not an observation with instrumentation. Academic work (Eck et al., FSE 2019 "Understanding flaky tests: the developer's perspective"; arXiv 2203.00483 survey on how flakiness affects developers) documents eroded trust and some reluctance to write tests, but establishes neither a 50% tipping point nor cessation of test-writing.

NON-SEQUITUR TO THE CONCLUSION. Even granting the anecdote, "flakiness erodes trust" is not evidence that detection + quarantine + burn-down TOOLING yields productivity gains; the cited source contains zero outcome data linking such tooling to any productivity measure. Note the directional phenomenon (flakiness erodes trust in the suite) is genuinely supported by academic literature — but the specific evidentiary chain this claim rests on (50%+ threshold, organizational collapse, "review cites organizations") does not survive scrutiny. AGE: a 2019 unquantified vendor anecdote, reviewed in 2022, being used in 2026 as a load-bearing roadmap justification.

verdicts.claim: 75% of flaky tests (184 of 245 studied) are already flaky at the commit that introduces the test, so running flaky-test detectors on newly added tests catches the large majority of flakiness at the moment it is cheapest to fix — a test-intelligence platform should therefore flag flakiness at test-introduction time (PR/first-run), not only after longitudinal history accumulates.
verdicts.evidence:
VERDICT: the raw statistic is verbatim-accurate, but the claim's actionable prescription is an overreach that the source itself contradicts, and the 245-test population is selected in a way that does not transfer to a CI-ingesting test-intelligence platform.

1) STATISTIC IS REAL (not disputed). I extracted the full text of the PDF. Abstract: "We apply two state-of-the-art detectors to 55 Java projects, identifying a total of 245 flaky tests that can be compiled and run in the code version where each test was added. We find that 75% of flaky tests (184 out of 245) are flaky when added." Peer-reviewed, Proc. ACM Program. Lang. Vol 4, OOPSLA, Article 202, Nov 2020 (Lam, Winter, Wei, Xie, Marinov, Bell). Sec. 10 repeats it. So checklist items 3 and 5 pass.

2) THE SOURCE EXPLICITLY CONTRADICTS "not only after longitudinal history accumulates." Sec. 8: "we suggest that developers run flaky-test detectors not only when tests are added or modified, but also with a minimum regular frequency (e.g., monthly)." Abstract: "running detectors solely on newly added tests would still miss detecting 25% of flaky tests." Sec. 5: "in some projects, all flaky tests were flaky on their TIC, and in others, none were" — wildfly/wildfly had 23 of 39 NOT flaky at introduction, and "7 projects with at least one test not detected actually have none of their tests detected in their TIC." The per-project rate ranges 0%-100%, so 75% is not a rate any single team can plan against.

3) SELECTION BIAS INFLATES THE 75% AND MAKES IT NON-TRANSFERABLE. Of 684 detected flaky tests only 432 were confirmed and only 245 (36%) form the denominator. The 252 unknown-dependent tests were excluded BY DESIGN — "We did not attempt to run unknown-dependent tests on their TIC: if we could not reproduce their flakiness even on the iDFlakies-commit..." i.e. the least reproducible, hardest-to-catch flakiness was removed from the denominator before computing the 75%. A further ~187 confirmed flaky tests were dropped because old commits would not compile (survivorship on buildable history).

4) THE POPULATION IS THE WRONG CATEGORY MIX FOR THIS PRODUCT. Table 2 totals row: of the 245, 113 are ID (NonDex / implementation-dependent, 46%), 99 are order-dependent (80 OD Vic + 19 OD Brit, 40%), and only 33 are ND (13%). ID and OD flakiness are intrinsic properties of the test/suite code, near-tautologically present at the introducing commit. The flakiness a report-ingesting platform actually observes (timing/async/network/environment = ND) is n=33 here. The authors concede the detector bias themselves: "252 of the 684 flaky tests that we detected were unknown-dependent... This result shows the need for the community to develop new flaky-test detectors that do not focus on order or implementation dependence." Threats to validity: "the flaky tests that we study come from only two detectors."

5) "PR/FIRST-RUN" IS A MISREAD OF WHAT THE PAPER RECOMMENDS. The paper's "run detectors on newly added tests" means active, instrumented detection campaigns — iDFlakies randomized-order rerun campaigns plus NonDex bytecode-level shuffling (NonDex run 10x per module at level ONE), plus One-By-One polluter search. It does NOT mean flagging flakiness from a first observed CI run. An OD victim passes deterministically in the shipped order and is undetectable from ingested JUnit/Playwright results at any number of first runs. Gruber et al., "An Empirical Study of Flaky Tests in Python" (ICST 2021, arXiv:2101.09077; 22,352 projects, 876,186 tests) find ~170 reruns on average are needed for 95% confidence that a passing test is not flaky — so "at the moment it is cheapest" is unsupported on the detection-cost side; it is only cheap on the fix side.

6) INDEPENDENT QUALIFICATION. "Systemic Flakiness: An Empirical Analysis of Co-Occurring Flaky Test Failures" (arXiv:2504.16777, 2025) reports flaky failures cluster (clusters averaging 13.5 tests) with predominant causes being "intermittent networking issues and instabilities in external dependencies" — environment-level root causes that are not properties of the introducing commit and cannot be surfaced by per-test introduction-time detection.

BOTTOM LINE FOR THE ROADMAP: usable as "budget an active order-shuffling/instrumented detection campaign against newly added and directly modified tests (85% figure), AND keep periodic re-detection, because per-project yield ranges 0-100% and environment-caused flakiness is invisible at introduction." NOT usable as stated — "flag flakiness at PR/first-run, not only after longitudinal history" would license a feature that cannot detect the order-dependent and environment-dependent flakiness that dominates real CI ingest. Age (2020) is acceptable for this finding but the Java/Maven/OSS scope and the two-detector scope are load-bearing limits the claim drops.

verdicts.claim: Extending detection to directly modified tests raises coverage to 85%, but the remaining 15% of flaky tests become flaky due to changes made elsewhere (code under test, other tests, dependencies) and can only be caught by continuously applying detection to all tests — meaning new/modified-test-only strategies (as used at Mozilla and Netflix) have a measurable, quantified blind spot.
verdicts.evidence:
VERDICT: Quote is verbatim and correctly attributed, but the claim strips every scope qualifier that makes the 85/15 numbers meaningful. Refuted as an over-generalization, not as a fabrication.

WHAT CHECKS OUT (verified against the actual PDF, extracted via pypdf, 29pp):
- The supporting quote is verbatim from the abstract (p.202:1, lines 25-28): "The percentage of flaky tests that can be detected does increase to 85% when detectors are run on newly added or directly modified tests. The remaining 15% of flaky tests become flaky due to other changes and can be detected only when detectors are always applied to all tests."
- The Mozilla/Netflix attribution is the paper's own framing, not the claim's invention. Abstract: "Some software organizations, e.g., Mozilla and Netflix, run some tools—detectors—to detect flaky tests as soon as possible... these organizations typically run a detector solely on newly added or directly modified tests."
- Body derivation is explicit (Sec. 6): 184 flaky-when-added + 24 of 61 that became flaky via a change to the test class = "208 of 245 (85%)". The 15% "become flaky due to changes not being directly in the test class itself but rather elsewhere in the test suite, code under test, or library dependencies" — matching the claim's parenthetical exactly.
- Source quality is strong: OOPSLA/PACMPL 2020 (Lam, Winter, Wei, Xie, Marinov, Bell), top-tier peer-reviewed primary source. Not marketing, not a vendor benchmark. Luo et al. FSE 2014 independently found 78% flaky-when-added, corroborating rather than contradicting. I found no source disputing the figures.

WHY IT IS STILL REFUTED — the denominator is a narrow, self-selected subpopulation:
1. 245 is 36% of the detected corpus. The paper detected 684 potentially flaky tests, confirmed 432, and analyzed 245. Critically (Sec. 5): "We did not attempt to run unknown-dependent tests on their TIC." 252 of 684 tests (37%) were unknown-dependent and excluded BY DESIGN; threats-to-validity confirms they categorized tests as UD "to prevent such tests from affecting the results of our research questions." The 85/15 split is computed only over order-dependent + implementation-dependent tests that survived compilation on an old commit.
2. The excluded categories are exactly the practitioner-relevant ones. Only two detectors were used — iDFlakies (test-order) and NonDex (non-deterministic API implementations). The paper's own discussion lists "random numbers, network, timing, concurrency, or I/O" as flakiness sources "that still remain to be addressed," and says the UD result "shows the need for the community to develop new flaky-test detectors that do not focus on order or implementation dependence." For a platform ingesting Cypress/Playwright/pytest E2E results, where async-wait/timing/network flakiness dominates (Luo et al. 2014: async wait 45%, concurrency 20%), the 15% figure is measured on a nearly disjoint population.
3. The paper itself disowns the number's stability. External validity (Sec. 8.1.3): projects came from the iDFlakies dataset, "therefore our results may be biased the same way that our previous results may be biased (e.g., finding OD tests more frequent than they really are)." And Sec. 8: "this result varies across projects: in some projects, all flaky tests were flaky on their TIC, and in others, none were." A statistic ranging from 0% to 100% across projects is not a "measurable, quantified blind spot" a roadmap can size against — it is a corpus average over 55 Maven/Java projects.
4. Currency of the industry sub-claim. "As used at Mozilla and Netflix" is asserted in the present tense but rests on two citations: MozillaChaosMode (a 2019 wiki page) and NetflixAutomationTalk (a 2017 conference talk) — now 7 and 9 years old. No evidence was found that either org still runs this strategy unchanged.
5. "Can only be caught by continuously applying detection to all tests" is a 2020 framing. It predates prediction-based approaches that avoid exhaustive reruns (FlakeFlagger 2021, Flakify 2021, ML/code-evolution predictors 2023), so "only" is too strong today.

USABLE FORM: the directional finding survives — new/modified-test-only detection provably misses tests that turn flaky from external changes, so a detector strategy gated on test-file diffs has a real blind spot. The specific 85/15 quantification does not transfer outside order- and implementation-dependent Java flakiness and should not be cited as a sizing number.
verdicts.counterSource: Primary source self-refutation (Lam et al., OOPSLA 2020, https://mir.cs.illinois.edu/marinov/publications/LamETAL20LongitudinalFlakyTests.pdf): Sec. 5 "We did not attempt to run unknown-dependent tests on their TIC" (252 of 684 tests, 37%, excluded); Sec. 8.1.3 external validity "our results may be biased the same way that our previous results may be biased (e.g., finding OD tests more frequent than they really are)"; Sec. 8 "this result varies across projects: in some projects, all flaky tests were flaky on their TIC, and in others, none were"; Sec. 8 discussion naming "random numbers, network, timing, concurrency, or I/O" as sources "that still remain to be addressed." Corroborating context: Luo et al., FSE 2014 (https://mir.cs.illinois.edu/lamyaa/publications/fse14.pdf) category distribution (async wait 45%, concurrency 20%, test-order 12%) shows the study corpus omits the dominant real-world flakiness categories. Industry sub-claim rests on MozillaChaosMode (2019 wiki) and NetflixAutomationTalk (2017 talk).
